utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everybody. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner, Tom Hannis, and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, Ms. Tatjana Savic, and Ms. Deirdre Montgomery appearing for the Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Aleksandar Aleksic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we invite counsel for the first accused to open, I understand -- well, the Chamber has one or two housekeeping matters, but before we turn to that, we have been alerted that the OTP has a matter to raise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do and we thought it right to raise it before the official start of the Defence case. It relates back to the evidence of Witness ST-210, who was the witness, the summary witness, who dealt with the police log-books, the KU log-books. Your Honour, during the course of his cross-examination, he was shown some documents which were subsequently exhibited on the basis that these -- that the documents which were criminal reports did not appear in the log-books, and ergo, the log-books were defective. Your Honours may recall, there was some discussion about this. Mr. Olmsted who was dealing with the witness said that regrettably it had been discovered just before the witness came to give evidence that one page from the log-books, the Doboj log-book was missing. It was subsequently retrieved. It has been translated and it's already added to e-court. The Defence and the Trial Chamber were notified on the 17th of February of this year, so after we closed our case, and it was uploaded into e-court under 65 ter number 10493A, and indeed, Your Honours granted leave for the corrected crime register to be substituted. Now what that showed was this, Your Honour, that four of the documents which Mr. Zecevic put to him, which are 1D355, 1D356, 1D357, and 1D362 all appear on that missing page. And so the suggestion made by Mr. Zecevic that they were not there is, in fact, as it transpires, incorrect. There were two further criminal reports which were Exhibit 1D360, and 1D361, which, again, the suggestion was that these had been -- these did not appear in the crime register. In fact, when a check was made, as we were reviewing the evidence after the close of our case, it was seen that they did, in fact, appear on the second page. What had happened was that those two crime reports had simply omitted the KU number. Your Honours, we have sent this -- we sent a letter to Mr. Zecevic and Mr. Krgovic about this matter on the 15th of March and asked if they would be prepared to stipulate to this. Your Honours, it is important because obviously we rely for a number of reasons on these KU registers. And Your Honours, in fact, dealt with it, if I can just refer Your Honours to -- or mentioned it. Judge Hall started this by saying effectively was it correct that these entries, therefore, that the log-books were defective in this sense because these crime reports did not appear. And Judge Harhoff, at page 13769, stated: "But the Presiding Judge's remark a while ago still stands, namely, that evidence has been provided to show that the KU log-book in itself is incomplete, to understand the full picture." And I think this is accepted by the Chamber. Well, Your Honours it is now clear that's not right. Certainly not as far as those documents are concerned. We invited the Defence -- we've not had a response from Mr. Krgovic, but we invited Mr. Zecevic to simply make an admission or stipulation, as the Americans call it, that that was the case. He declines to do so. So, Your Honours, there are three options. The first is that we can apply to re-call Witness ST-210, simply to deal with this, which seems to us to be a complete waste of time. Second, we can take a statement from him under 92 bis and simply seek to put that in. Or, third, Your Honours can simply take note of the fact although it's -- in a sense it's me giving evidence, but I'm showing Your Honours where it can be seen in the books. So those are the options in the absence -- of course, we can't force either Defence team to agree to this, but we would suggest that this is something that clearly needs to be dealt with in some form or another before the Defence case starts, if at all possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, did I understand your third option to mean that a proper examination of the record would -- without the need for anything else, solve the -- indicate that what appeared to be a problem is not a problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Absolutely. The trouble is, of course, if one -- whoever -- if somebody for the purposes of the judgement would just happen to be reading the actual transcript, they would be misled. And provided all are satisfied with my explanation about this, so that it -- and -- and obviously this record is here now, and it can be seen by simply checking the documents, well, Your Honours, that seems to us to be sufficient. It would be preferable, and I understand Mr. Zecevic accepts that, if we could get agreement from the Defence and the -- on both sides. But failing that, it seems to me that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'd certainly hear what Mr. Zecevic has to say on this point. But if I understand you correctly, it may that be it would be sufficient for the -- this matter to abide such submissions as the Prosecution makes at the close of the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. What we don't want -- can I put it this way, we'd rather not have to waste time in our final brief or -- not so much time, but page numbers, because we will have a limit on how long the brief can be, on something which we would hope was agreed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, let me hear whether Mr. Zecevic has had a change of mind since his last communication with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I share the view of Your Honours that the -- this is more appropriate for the closing submissions of the Office of the Prosecutor than at this point in time. Now, I'm not sure what -- what the Office of the Prosecution is proposing. If they are proposing to re-open their case, there is a jurisprudence about that, and -- and they should apply for the -- for the re-opening of their case. If that is the -- if my understanding is correct of the position of the Office of the Prosecutor. However, Your Honours, the position of Defence doesn't change. We still maintain our position that the KU log-books are -- for obvious reasons and for a number of reasons are not sufficient for establishing these facts. The second problem is not only the KU books but this witness was asked to prepare an annex to his statement where he was on the instruction of the Office of the Prosecutor putting some numbers on the number of criminal reports filed against -- where the victims are non-Serbs and the perpetrators are Serbs. And we say that this -- that that annex is flawed. Therefore, there is no way that the Defence will stipulate to anything of the sort and we -- we maintain our position. And we will maintain it until the end of the case. And you will hear our evidence about that matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Do I understand you to essentially agree that, notwithstanding the -- what you have just articulated as to the effect of the evidence that is at present before us, it is, at the end of the day, a matter of what is made of that evidence and, therefore, it is probably not necessary to re-call the witness but that the whole thing can be left for, despite the reservations Ms. Korner may have about the -- how this would add to the bulk of material that we would have to consider, that at the end of the day it is still a question of argument between counsel for Defence on one side and counsel for Prosecution on the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Definitely, Your Honours. That is what I said at the very beginning. I just wanted to clarify my position why I say that. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, could I just ask, then, concretely in respect of these, was it five documents, six documents, would it be a problem for the Defence to accept that those were, in fact, in the KU log-books, while you can still maintain that the general picture of the KU log-books is still, in your view, that these books are insufficient? With or without those six documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Your Honours, I tried to explain. It is the not problem with the KU log-books by itself. It is the problem that the witness -- what -- looking at these KU log-books, not for this municipality but other municipalities, was preparing an annex and we say the annex is flawed. And the Office of the Prosecutor relies on his findings as a summary witness reviewing the KU log-books. Your Honours, it is a very simple situation. We are having as our witness the chief of the CSB Doboj, as you know. And it's our first witness and he will deal with this matter, I can guarantee that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I'm sorry, Mr. Zecevic is -- and I'm afraid, in our view, deliberately not answering the question. It is a very simple question. Whatever submissions we make about the efficiency of these books or otherwise, does the Defence, having had a chance to examine the documents which are exhibits, agree that those six crime reports exhibited with the numbers that I have given are actually in the KU book? Everything else, I agree, is for submissions. But that is a very simple, straightforward question which I would invite Your Honours to ask Mr. Zecevic and, of course, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I stated very clearly, I'm not ready to stipulate. And you will understand why I'm not ready to stipulate once you hear the evidence that we are going to present, Your Honours. And it is -- and after -- at the end of the day, this is a matter for the final submissions, definitely. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, I suppose you'll say otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... joint submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could counsel assist on a matter which, we confess, we -- you probably said it and we just didn't get it. Are these six documents already part of the evidence or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, they are. They were all exhibited, Your Honour. They're 1D355 through to -- sorry, 355, 356, 357, 360, 361, and 362. They were all made exhibits on the basis, and it's very clear in the transcript, I haven't bothered you with the references, on the basis that these were not in the KU register.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So if I'm to understand this correctly, the only issue that now remains is to whether these six documents were or were not --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- in some of the log-books.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: They're shown -- four of them were in the first page, which regrettably we had to go back and get because it hadn't been copied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: From which log-book?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's the -- does Your Honour want the exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's the Doboj crime register.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Which is the KU log-book.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The KU -- I'm sorry, yea. The KU log-book. I'm so sorry. Two of them were in fact already and could have been seen but the witness, I imagine rather taken by surprise -- in fact he does say at some stage, "I would like to a chance to review this." And indeed they are mentioned in his report, and that's 1D360 and 1D361. But obviously giving evidence, it was rather [indiscernible]. As I say, all I'm asking for is that the Defence who have had the opportunity -- we sent the letter on the 15th of March, appreciating that Mr. Zecevic has had a lot to do recently, but we did ask for an answer. My understanding was it isn't disputed. It can be seen. It is clear, but he is not prepared to stipulate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the KU log-book is also Exhibit 1D, 1D Exhibit, 358. So, therefore, we offered also the KU log-book as our exhibit. And I don't really understand if all these exhibits are inside the -- the material in this case, everybody can -- can, at the end of the day, take its own conclusions after we finish presenting evidence. Your Honours, if we start -- if we start stipulating on the issues in this case, we can -- we can adjourn and meet after four months from now, because I will have a number of issues that I would ask the Office of the Prosecutor to stipulate at this point. I don't really understand -- I don't understand the -- the reasoning behind ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the reasoning is that the transcript, if read, would be misleading. That's why. And as it is misleading, we think the correction should be agreed. It is not agreement or a stipulation to our case which -- as to what the log-books show. Its relevance to the issues. It's a simple stipulation to a factual matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, now I think I begin to understand Mr. Zecevic's point. Because, are you saying that, if these six documents were accepted as actually having been properly inscribed in that particular KU log-book, then the log-book would be completely reliable and exhaustive.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... I'm saying that that is a matter of argument which we may or may not make at the end of the case. I'm simply saying that at the present time, you admitted these particular documents or these particular documents were admitted on the basis that they were not shown in the Prosecution log-book. All I'm saying is that they were admitted under -- and I'm not saying that -- that -- that it's done deliberately. We didn't have the first page and to that extent it was our fault. But now that we do, now it's been admitted into evidence, all I'm pointing out is that certainly four of the documents -- in fact all six were admitted on a false basis; namely, that they were not reflected in the log-book. And all I'm asking for is for a clear, simple, straightforward admission that if you look at the log-book, those criminal reports are recorded, which will save everybody an awful lot of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We -- we are grateful to counsel for seeking to enlighten us on this matter. And it appears to us that -- what Ms. Korner has indicated as option 3 is the practical way forward.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, yes, I'm just sorry that -- that the Defence don't feel able to assist everybody in this court in this way. Your Honour, there is one other -- or two other matters. First is this. Recently we provided to the Defence some information relating to Dr. Nielsen, which came to the attention Mr. Hannis and myself relatively recently. We have been asking Mr. Zecevic whether he wishes to deal with this matter at all, and, at the moment, I understand he does not, but may file something later this week. I'm sorry again that it's not possible to deal with this orally, if at all. Your Honour, the difficulty raises is this. They have now given us their expert's report. We would obviously wish to seek Dr. Nielsen's take on it. It's a very lengthy report. We've, so far, not done that because, obviously in case Mr. Zecevic wanted to raise anything, we felt we ought to wait. But because -- and we've been asking Mr. Zecevic for some time now, because he hasn't, can I just say this. We are going to send him -- I'm not asking Your Honours to do. This is simply so the Court's informed. We are going to send him Professor Bajagic's report to seek his comments on it. We can't wait any longer because, subject to Your Honours' ruling on Mr. Zecevic's application for reconsideration, we haven't got that much time left. Your Honours, finally, we were given on Friday night -- four -- well, no, I mean a total -- some more documents, some of which are not on the 65 ter list, to be used with Mr. Bjelosevic. Four of them don't have translations. And, Your Honours, I'm really sorry, but we have to know in advance what it is the Defence are going to use. And it may well be that if this goes on, we will be saying, again, we will not be in a position to cross-examine and the witness will have to go away and come back again. We've been given already a 150-odd documents for this witness, so I'm -- we simply must have translations. I shouldn't -- as I say, some of these documents are not on the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I may respond, Your Honours. On the first matter, we intend to file a written submission concerning this situation with Dr. Nielsen. And I hope you will appreciate that we were rather busy preparing the opening statement and the first witness and, therefore, we couldn't -- we couldn't file that earlier. So this is -- this will be filed within next 24 to 48 hours. And we needed to check some of the information which the Office of the Prosecution provided to us. The second matter, Your Honours, we came in the possession of these documents the day when we disclosed it to the -- to the Office of the Prosecutor. They're not on our 65 ter list. We just disclosed it as a matter of courtesy that these documents have been received and we immediately disclosed to them the documents. We sent the documents for translation. Whether we are going to use those documents and if we are going to -- to ask leave to add them to 65 ter list remains to be seen. If we do, then -- then this -- then this opposition by Office of the Prosecutor would be -- would be justified. At this point, I don't think -- maybe we are not going to use the documents. We just disclosed them to the Office of the Prosecutor as a matter of courtesy. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, except that the e-mail that came with them said, "These are documents we propose to use." That's why I raised it. If they were simply disclosed to us, I wouldn't have bothered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So they over-spoke in the e-mail.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: They over-spoke in the e-mail.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Your apprehension is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I can only go on what I'm told. I'm afraid I rather feel that it's an excuse rather than anything else, but let's see where we go. But, Your Honours, I'm just giving notice that if this goes on like this, we will be seeking an adjournment before cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we will see when we arrive at that point. Thank you. There are one or two housekeeping matters which the Chamber would wish to raise. The first relates to the witness Bajagic who is scheduled to testify on the 2nd of May, and the Chamber's preference is that he begins testifying on the indicated date. And the -- as of Friday - I don't know whether things have changed after to this morning - there still remain two documents that remain to be disclosed, and we would ask the Prosecution if it accepts to have this witness begin on the 2nd of May even though it would be less than 30 days' from the last disclosure of the complete material. As for the decision on the expertise of Mr. Bajagic, the Chamber notes Ms. Korner's statements at the Pre-Defence Conference that the Prosecution does not dispute his expertise regarding the MUP. The Prosecution has, however, raised objections regarding certain parts of his report which it submits lies outside of his expertise, and it is noted the Prosecution would file its observations in advance of the 2nd of May. Accordingly, the matter of whether, and if so which, parts of the report will be admitted into evidence will, as has been the practice up to this point, be decided at the conclusion of the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I may be of assistance, just an update on the matter of translations. The draft translations have been provided to the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. The second matter relates to the OTP request on the 270 new death certificates and we give an oral ruling as follows. At the Pre-Defence Conference on the 4th of April, the Prosecution stated that it had obtained 270 death certificates in B/C/S which it would seek to add to the consolidated hyperlinked spreadsheet or proof of death database which the Chamber admitted into evidence by its decision of the 1st of February. In order to be able to assess properly this matter, the Chamber directs the Prosecution to file a written motion which is to include: One, English translations of all the materials the Prosecution requests the Chamber to consider; and two, an updated spreadsheet which includes the new material. With reference to the Stanisic Defence submission on the 4th of April, that there remains pending an oral application by the Defence to reconsider the Chamber's decision of the 1st of February, the Chamber finds no record that such a request was ever made and therefore need not further consider this submission. The final matter -- sorry, you wanted to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... something about the translations. What we've done, all the death certificates are on the same form. So we're having one translated in full, and then for the rest, all that will be translated are the details, the name, date of birth, and so on and so forth. Because to translate 270 documents identical documents in full would, we hope, be somewhat otiose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I may say so, Ms. Korner, it appears eminently sensible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- of course, the -- each of these items would have to be linked to the spreadsheet. That's the practical [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Chamber is in receipt of the batting order for the first two months with estimates for the examination-in-chief and it would be useful for us to receive cross-examination estimates, especially for the witness who is scheduled to begin tomorrow. And the -- that matter -- there's a usual segue into a related issue of which counsel may have been -- to which counsel may have been alerted, and it is this. Up to this point, we have been operating on the assumption that once the Defence opens, that this trial will continue at the pace of five hearings, five days a week. Come the middle of June or thereabouts, it probably wouldn't arise before that, two members of this Bench having been assigned to another matter, it would mean that the hearing five days a week in this once case would not be possible. So it remains to be seen, and the e-mail -- there is, I believe, an e-mail in circulation inviting counsel in both cases with which we are concerned, their input into how to stagger the presentation of the cases to accommodate the fact that -- that Judges have overlapping duties. But, as I said, we seem to be clear for the first -- for the time being. But this would arise come sometime in June. So unless there are any further matters, I would -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, no, Your Honour, I was only going to say that if it is in circulation, it hasn't circulated to us yet. But, as regards the estimate for the first witness, certainly the 20 hours proposed by Mr. Zecevic for his examination-in-chief and particularly in the light of the recent discussions about the Doboj log-books which I note, by the way, is not on the list of documents that the Defence propose to use, so I was interested to hear that Mr. Bjelosevic was supposed to be dealing with this. Your Honours, it will be exactly the same amount from the Prosecution. I understand that Mr. Krgovic says that he is going to be an hour and a half with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So we invite counsel for Mr. Stanisic to open.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. In order to be very precise, I will speak in Serbian. Thank you very much. [Interpretation] Your Honours, I shall start my opening statement in this case by firstly speaking about the context surrounding the events which are the subject of these proceedings. In order to properly understand the causes and consequences as well as the developments that took place in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina during the period relevant to the indictment, the situation must be put in a proper context. The Prosecution spoke about the context of the events in the indictment, firstly in the opening statement and then during the entire Prosecution case. The Defence believes that the Prosecution described the context in overly simplified terms or, rather, that their description of the context, whether deliberate or not, was by -- based on the secondary phenomena and consequences of less important processes that took place. In that sense, the context was used to justify the conclusions and the theory of the Prosecution case. During the Defence case, the Defence intends to lead evidence which will paint an objective picture of the context based on the fundamental processes that took place in society, and by that I mean the former Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, because we believe that this aspect of the case is the important background which will allow us all to better understand the events that ensued and that have since become the object of this indictment. I will take this opportunity to briefly outline some of the significant social processes which, in the Defence's view, created a context relevant for the understanding of this case. As a federal union of six republics and two autonomous provinces, both in the Republic of Serbia, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was created during the World War II or the National Liberation War as it was known in the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Its social and political constitution was reflected in the name of the state as socialist, in that the ideology was undoubtedly Communist. The social and political constitution was further characterised by a mono-party system dominated by a party which was initially known as the Communist party of Yugoslavia and thereafter as the League of Communists of Yugoslavia. The state consisted of several nations which is why the aspects of nation and nationality were given a lot of attention. One of the underlying causes of that attention were the historical events and conflicts between members of different ethnic groups in the area, especially during the Second World War whose consequences were still fresh in everybody's member. In a desire to overcome possible major problems, including the problem of time which would have been required to establish the guilt of individuals and groups for the events that had taken place during the Second World War as well as to eliminate the causes of such events, the Communist leadership of the state decided to make the leap of faith and establish a society based on the concepts such as were -- the brotherhood and unity of all the nations and nationalities that resided in the territory of the SFRY and similar equally empty phrases. Besides offering practical benefits to the then-government, that decision was in keeping with the Communist ideology which was based, first and foremost, on class struggle and attachment to a class rather than to an ethnic group or tradition. Communist ideology disparages national traditions and ethnic affiliations; i.e., it doesn't recognise any of those because it advocates Communist internationalism. In some cases and in some parts of the state, that way of dealing with this issue as adopted by the government and the party certainly required harsh repressive measures during the first 10- or 15-year period after the end of the Second World War. After that period, any public display of national ideology was subject to uncompromising criminal prosecution. As a result, the problem of previous ethnic conflicts among the peoples of the SFRY seemed to have been solved, and save for a small number of dissents who continued to pursue the matter, the problem was largely ignored by the official authorities. However, the problem continued to persist, and the memories of the events that had taken place during the Second World War were passed on among family members or in smaller local circles. As is often the case, since the memories of those events were suppressed by force, i.e., by the state enforcement agencies, they became mystified in the collective memory of individuals and national groups. The entire political and legal system of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was based, as I've already said it, on a mono-party system in which the party played a regulatory role of sorts. I dare even say that it had a controlling role over any social, political or economic processes that were taking place in society. Let me explain this. Through its local bodies and branches, the League of Communists exerted its influence in all spheres of life. In that way, the party exerted a significant influence on the choice of cadres for all positions. I dare say in the local bodies of government, municipalities and cities, all the way up to the Federation. It also influenced the choice of cadres in the economy, judiciary, state administration, education, health system, military, and so on. The situation changed in 1990, with the onset of democratisation and the introduction of a multi-party system. A large number of political parties were created overnight. They sprung up like mushrooms after the rain, which is only understandable because the same kind of processes were taking place across Europe during the period of post-Communist transition. However, the situation changed only on the face of it but essentially it remained the same. As illustrated and confirmed by numerous examples in recent past, by that I mean Iraq and Afghanistan, the introduction of a multi-party system and the democratisation of a society is a process and not a simple declaration of the fact. Such a process, necessarily means that the population must be educated about the functioning and democratic principles. It especially implies the creation of bodies and putting in place a structure compatible with such a democratic system. None of that existed in the former Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. In some more developed parts where some sort of democratic traditions were in place, like, for example, the Republic of Slovenia or larger economic centres, the system started to undergo the process of transformation, but if anything, the transformation was only skin deep and purely cosmetic. The structure of the political and legal system had not changed nor was that objectively possible within such a short period of time. As a result, the HDZ and the SDS parties in Croatia and Serbia respectively were given to play an identical role as the defeated League of Communists before that. All the other parties mostly served as choreography. I believe that it is a widely known fact that both Franjo Tudjman, the HDZ leader in Croatia, and Slobodan Milosevic, the SDS leader in Serbia, were proven Communists. Tudjman as a JNA general and Milosevic as a high-ranking party leader. Since the two of them were undoubtedly very close to the Communist ideology and they were also rather familiar with the functioning of the League of Communists, the respective parties that they headed were modelled after the League of Communists in terms of their organisation, structure, and functioning. Only a relatively low number of intellectuals at the time saw democratisation in the proper sense of the term, i.e., as a possibility to create institutions based on the rule of democracy, law, and free from party control in all segments of life and work. Unfortunately, their numbers were low in the entire territory of the former Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia and they were marginalised in every sense which made it impossible for them to fight against the populous parties and movements that ended up imposing themselves on the large popular masses. The emergence of democracy and the break up with Communism led to the abolishment of all taboo topics, so the national issue which was previously strictly controlled and carefully concealed, unfortunately came to the fore. All the leading parties in the republics displayed very pronounced national self-awareness. The surge of that national awareness, which to a certain extent could be seen as a consequence and product of the fact that the issue had been largely ignored as non-existent by the Communist authorities for a number of years, did not move things in a positive direction. Unfortunately, quite the contrary was true. That national self-awareness assumed the characteristics of national exclusivity and chauvinism. One of the plausible underlying reasons for that was the desire of all those parties to make themselves popular, which was a reaction to Communism, and to give prominence to those issues which had been either ignored or prohibited during the Communist rule. Since all the parties based their programmes on the same identical issues, their positions gradually became more radical in an attempt to attract the highest possible number of voters. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, which had been a known as a small Yugoslavia due to its specific characteristics, those tendencies resulted in even more pronounced consequences as citizens sided with their own national parties. The reason for that probably lies in the relative underdevelopment of Bosnia and Herzegovina, even the backwardness of some of its parts, in the structure of the population, the history and the ostensible absence of any democratic traditions in the area. It is already in evidence that the breakdown of the Ottoman Empire after the Berlin Congress that took place in 1878 left Bosnia and Herzegovina a rather underdeveloped state in the region. It remained underdeveloped as a short-lived protectorate of the Habsburg Monarchy towards the end of the 19th century. In 1907, it was annexed by the Habsburg Monarchy which meant that the area was again occupied, although under rather different principles in respect of the Ottoman occupation. It can be said that only then, at the beginning of the 20th century, the Habsburg occupation planted the seeds of democracy in Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, that was again very short lived. During the World War I, the Habsburg Monarchy collapsed and after the end of the war, the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina became part of the kingdom of the Serbs, Croats and Slovenians first and then Yugoslavia, and finally, after the Second World War, Communists took power. Since the national structure of the population of Bosnia and Herzegovina was not homogenous, the only option to stand up against the League of Communists was to create a coalition of ethnic parties because without such a coalition, it was impossible to win a majority of votes in Bosnia and Herzegovina and beat the League of Communists at elections. Unfortunately, this type of coalition with victory over Communism being a common denominator of all the coalition parties was doomed from the very outset. Namely, all those ethnic parties, just like the HDZ in Croatia, and the SBS in Serbia, were essentially anti-democratic, and as I've already stated, they mirrored the League of Communists and modelled themselves after it. This was especially true of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina which was undoubtedly part of the HDZ of Croatia, and as such, it implemented the policies of the mother republic and its leading party and it was directly subordinated to the party leader and president of Croatia, Franjo Tudjman. One of the instantly recognisable characteristics of all ethnic parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina was the fact that they copied the work of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia in the sense that each of them wanted to grab as many resources for themselves and to take as much control as possible over the institutions of power. As I've stated already, there were no democratic or structural mechanisms in place to prevent them from doing so, because the system that existed and that was inherited was based exclusively on a mono-party system. A special problem in Bosnia and Herzegovina was the fact that ethnic parties, or at least their original leaderships, or those that were the first to join them, were mostly people with little or no experience in the matters of politics or state administration. In that sense, unlike the HDZ in Croatia, or the SBS in Serbia, where most of the members had joined from the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, the lack of competency was particularly pronounced among the ethnic parties of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Your Honours, I believe that during the Prosecution case you saw ample evidence testifying to that lack of competency among the people in leading positions. Poorly educated people were appointed to responsible positions in the state apparatus, in political bodies and the state administration in general. Even if there were any with higher education, as a rule their educational background had nothing to do with the positions to which they were appointed and the roles they played. People with no experience or knowledge were appointed to positions in political institutions, municipalities, and the state administration. During the Prosecution case, we were given as an example a municipality where the president of the Executive Council, the chief of the SJB and the chief of the Secretariat of National Defence were all engineers. I believe that they had degrees in either physics or chemistry and they didn't have any prior work experience. As you know, the MUP -- the Ministry of Interior at the state level was not much different in terms of its leadership. A large majority of the Assembly members, as you may be able to conclude from the evidence in this case, in the Assembly of the Republika Srpska, for example, were novices to the job. Their discussions were often offensive, inappropriate and not very productive either. A very specific characteristic of Bosnia and Herzegovina of which you will hear more in the future, although there has been much evidence to that effect already in this case, is the fact that the three ethnic political parties deliberately or by chance polarised the population along the ethnic rather than political lines. From the moment they were created, they considered themselves the only legitimate representatives of the ethnic group they represented and that is how they conducted their business. The ultimate result of that is -- is that even now, before at this Tribunal, somebody's ethnic affiliation is often considered the same as their party affiliations. If you're a Serb, then you're also the SDS. A Croat is also the HDZ, and a Muslim is the SDA although it doesn't necessarily have to be true. Nor should this be indeed be the case because an individual's political affiliations should depend on the party's programme and the individual's preference and interests. You have also heard that all smaller parties ceased to exist or became marginalised as a result of that. Whereas the SDA, HDZ and SDS coalition which initially favoured party members as their candidates for various positions given to them based on the -- the inter-party agreement but later on, faced with a shortage of party members to fill those positions, they started appointed individuals based on their ethnic rather than party affiliations. Primarily for these reasons, the legal system and structures of power simply collapsed in the entire territory of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia and particularly in Bosnia and Herzegovina, as you will see. As a result, laws were being broken every step of the way and at all levels, from the Federation and Republics to the municipalities. In Bosnia and Herzegovina this may be illustrated by various examples starting with the establishment of the SDA as an ethnic party and then other ethnic parties, although that was strictly forbidden under the laws then prevailing in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The process culminated in October 1992, when, contrary to the valid constitution and the legal regulations of Bosnia and Herzegovina, a declaration of independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina was passed by the SDA and HDZ members of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Assembly in the absence of the representatives of the Serbian people. In one of his statements, Lord Carrington said that that act, undoubtedly initiated by Alija Izetbegovic, was illegal. Can we now play the video please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: "... have been in the majority. And then the Muslims, who had a very much higher birthrate than the Serbs became the predominant -- the majority of the population. And this, of course, was something very hard for the Serbs to swallow, and they made it abundantly plain very early on that they were not prepared to accept the situation in which there was an independent Bosnia under the constitution which then prevailed, and indeed under the institution that then prevailed, it was not -- it was illegal for Izetbegovic to declare independence because any constitutional change of that magnitude had to be agreed by all three parties."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. During the Defence case, you will see how far-reaching the state of lawlessness in Bosnia and Herzegovina was and how slowly but surely it led to legal and political chaos. You will see that the impotence of the central powers in Sarajevo resulted in the regional associations of municipalities which had almost nothing to do with the central republican powers. Some associated themselves with their mother states, like, for example, the community of Herceg-Bosnia, which was in the western part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, leaned on Croatia. Some leaned on the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, i.e., the Federation, like, for example, the Autonomous Region of Krajina in north-western Bosnia, whereas some existed on their own. The impotence of the state apparatus and its structures top down to the local level was partly due to the lack of competence of its leaders who even if they had wanted to stop those processes, probably simply didn't know how to do it. This fact, which I consider extremely important for the sequence of events that ensued, has already been corroborated by ample evidence led during the Prosecution case. The Defence will lead other evidence to that effect. When armed conflicts started to take place in the atmosphere that I have just described, the situation became absolutely unbearable and impossible for the functioning of the state and its united powers, as you will see from the documents and evidence we intend to exhibit. And now led me say something about Mr. Mico Stanisic. The evidence that was led during the Prosecution case shows the following. Mico Stanisic was born to an impoverished patriarchal family that lived off agriculture and cattle breeding in Ponor village in Pale municipality, some 50 kilometres south-east of Sarajevo on the slopes of Mount Romanija.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm very sorry to interrupt, Mr. Zecevic, but that's not evidence we led, and as I understand it, Mr. Zecevic is not calling Mr. Stanisic. Is he saying that's evidence that's going to be given by somebody else?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. As I said, Ms. Korner, this is the evidence which you -- that you led in this case. It's P2300, P23 [Microphone not activated] those are the exhibits in this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I hear what Mr. Zecevic says, Your Honour. We'll check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stanisic's family had three children. The only way for a poor family to give their children education was to send them to military or police schools. After having enrolled in the police school in Sarajevo, Stanisic himself was a hard-working student. His hard work paid off and in the school year 1972/1973, he was proclaimed the best final-year student in all of Bosnia and Herzegovina, based on his achievements. He was also an active athlete. He trained judo, which made him popular and well-known in the city of Sarajevo. You will hear that he graduated from the secondary police school as the best student in his generation. After graduation he signed an employment contract with the Ministry of Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and enrolled at the law school in Sarajevo. While studying, he also held a permanent job and the cost of his education was borne by the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Defence will lead evidence to show that the colleagues always perceived Mico Stanisic as serious and hard-working. Somebody who always carried school-books around and took any opportunity to revise. You will also hear that he was a dedicated athlete and student, that he never drank and that he was never argumentative. You will also hear that from the very start of his career, he was always seen as a man of strong principles and a professional who always did everything by the book and insisted on respect for the laws and regulations. Also that he was sociable and that he socialised with members of all ethnicities, that from the age of 15 he shared a room in the dormitory of the police school with a Muslim and a Croat, his fellow students. Nobody ever saw or heard him display any nationalist feelings nor did he ever spoke offensively about members of any other ethnicity. On the contrary, he was considered a role model as the best member of the youth organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In 1973, he had the honour of being the first to carry the relay race baton which was traditionally given to President Tito every year on his birthday, which was also a national holiday known as the day of youth, a holiday which symbolised the fraternity and unity of the peoples and the youth of Yugoslavia in the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. After a while, Mico Stanisic left the police and joined the business community as a successful manager of the Gradske Trznice Trading Company which supplied the city of Sarajevo with food. After the victory of ethnic parties at the 1990 elections, despite the support he enjoyed from the SDA, he left his position as company director because the support was conditional upon the shake-up of the staff. He was not willing to be involved in that because he believed that the company was not a state property and that the only parameters of the company's success were its performance and profit. From that moment on, he was in private business and together with his wife he opened several consumer goods shops. Towards the end of 1990, he joined the steering committee to establish the democratic party of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a true democratic party, where he worked together with the democratic parties of Serb Yugoslavia. That party was not an ethnic party nor did it have such aspirations. At the time, Professor Nenad Kecmanovic, a well-known intellectual and dissident during the Communist rule, was earmarked as the future party president. However, Kecmanovic joined the party of reformists led by the then prime minister Ante Markovic, while ethnic parties started being registers and the picture changed. Members of different ethnicities, almost to the last, started joining their own ethnic parties. When the Prosveta association, the club of Serbian intellectuals, which included Radovan Karadzic as its member, proposed to establish a Serbian ethnic party, a large number of small parties with majority Serbian memberships disappeared and their members joined the new SDS party. The party whose steering committee member was Mico Stanisic experienced the same fate. In July 1990, very soon after the establishment of the SDS, Mico Stanisic clashed with SDS members, and in early Autumn 1990, Mico Stanisic quit the political life and the party. In March 1991, at Vitomir Zepinic's proposal, Mico Stanisic returned to the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and joined as the secretary of the Sarajevo SUP. Although no other than Momcilo Krajisnik's brother Mirko was his counter-candidate for the position, Croat and Muslim support was the decisive factor in Mico Stanisic's appointment. You will hear that on his return to the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mico Stanisic continued to uphold his principles and insisted on the strict enforcement of the law, and that because of such position, he clashed with certain structures within the MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina with respect to the illegal issuance of identity cards and passports to individuals who were not BH citizens, and he was eventually removed from the position as the chief of the Sarajevo SUP. After that, on 14th of February, Mico Stanisic was appointed as an advisor to Minister Delimustafic. During the Defence case you will hear that the prime candidate for the post of the interior minister of the Republika Srpska after the promulgation of the constitution and the passing of the laws on internal affairs and on ministers and government was Vitomir Zepinic. However, his candidacy was withdrawn because of suspicions that he had been involved in illegal dealings together with Alija Delimustafic. After that, Prime Minister Djeric appointed Mico Stanisic as minister. You already heard during the Prosecution case that he accepted the appointment halfheartedly. And let me quote Prime Minister Djeric who said at the meeting of the Assembly at which he explained his proposals for the ministers of the interior and foreign affairs, this is Exhibit P198, page 4, Prime Minister Djeric said that Assembly meeting: "I would like to stress that both candidates certainly appreciate the current position of the Serbian people. I'm not saying that they have accepted the positions halfheartedly, but they have not refused them. So much about that." Those were Djeric's words uttered at that Assembly meeting. Speaking about the events of the 1st of March and barricades in Sarajevo, the evidence we will adduce will show that no MUP inspectors or operatives ever implicated Mico Stanisic in the events, nor was anybody in the MUP privy to information that Mico Stanisic had any role to play in those events, contrary to the Prosecutor's allegations. You will also hear that after his appointment as minister of the interior of the Republika Srpska, Mico Stanisic continued to insist on the consistent and strict implementation of the laws and regulations. He continued to be considered a man of principles when it came to enforcing the laws and insisting on the professional work of the police. He applied these principles indiscriminately to his own work as well as to the work of his associates. Your Honours, I have noted the time. It would be a good moment for me to make a break here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we will resume in 20 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We will -- may I continue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will have the video played, if we can have the transcripts given to the Trial Chamber and the Office of the Prosecutor. Madam Registrar? It's our second video. [Interpretation] Your Honours, before the break, I said that you would hear during the Defence case that even after the appointment as minister of the interior of Republika Srpska, Mico Stanisic, he continued to be considered a man of principles when it came to enforcing the law and insisting on the professional work of the police and that he applied his principles indiscriminately to his own work as well as to the work of his associates. To illustrate this, I will show you an authentic contemporary video-clip depicting the parade of the Sokolac police on the 30th of March, 1992, under Mico Stanisic's supervision. On that occasion, he held a speech. The video from Sokolac is 1D1 -- or, rather, that is the transcript, whereas, the videos are 2D1. And now we're going to play the video.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] The text of the solemn declaration will be read by the minister of the interior of the Serbian Autonomous Region of Romanija, Zoran Cvijetic. "I declare that I will perform the duty of an authorised official continuously and responsibility [as interpreted], that I will abide by the Constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Yugoslavia and the law, and that will I protect the constitutionality of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Yugoslavia, the rights, freedoms and security, and that I will carry out those and other tasks and assignments of an authorised official, even in cases when carrying out these tasks and assignments would bring my life into jeopardy. "The minister of the interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mico Stanisic, will address the members of the police units of the Serbian Autonomous Region of Romanija. "As of today, the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina has its own police force. The legality of our existence is provided by the constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Law on Internal Affairs which was recently adopted by the Assembly at its session. Moreover, the legality of our existence is based on the results of negotiations of the three ethnic communities under the auspices of the European community. As of today, we will act as the police of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which will carry out its tasks and assignments professionally and not politically, as the MUP of the old Bosnia and Herzegovina has done so far, in order to protect property, life, body, and other securities of all citizens in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina equally. "Members of the police, we are not involved in politics. We must carry out our tasks professionally. For those reasons, long speeches do not belong to us as of today. Good luck. Get to work in the interests of all who live in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Thank you."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. As you could see, Your Honours, during his first official appearance as interior minister, Mr. Mico Stanisic insisted that the police had a duty to protect the lives and property of all - I stress the word "all" because that word was stressed by Mr. Stanisic in his speech - "of all citizens of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." This is a rare example from that period, where the equality and protection of all citizens is stressed. As you all know already, that period was characterised by incendiary nationalistic speeches by state officials representing all the three national communities in Bosnia and Herzegovina. From the evidence adduced so far, you know that Mico Stanisic attended the meeting of the collegium of the minister of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 1st of April, 1992, where the practical issues of the division of the Ministry of the Interior were discussed. The other participants were representatives of all of three sides, Alija Delimustafic's assistants. Mico Stanisic participated in his capacity as minister, Delimustafic's advisor, and minister of the interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. During the Prosecution case it was shown that Mico Stanisic had met with Jusuf Pusina, chief of public security of the MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina, a member of the SDA, on the 3rd of April, 1992, to discuss possible options for a building that would house the MUP of Republika Srpska headquarters in the territory of the city of Sarajevo. The next meeting was scheduled for the 5th of April, 1992, at Holiday Inn hotel in Sarajevo at 1330 hours, and in the meantime, Mr. Pusina was supposed to consult with President Izetbegovic about the headquarters of the MUP. On that day, when Mico Stanisic was waiting for the meeting to start, Pusina first informed him that he would not be able to attend because he was involved in an investigation into the murder of a Serbian policeman in the Novi Grad police station that had happened the night before, and then an another piece of news arrived about a conflict in Vrace and the killing of two Serbian policemen. During the Prosecution case, you heard and saw a number of exhibits and ample evidence that demonstrated Stanisic's dedication to the establishment and functioning of the MUP in strict compliance with the law when the MUP of Republika Srpska was being established practically from scratch during an extremely difficult period. You also heard about his persistent work aimed at stabilising the situation in the Ministry of the Interior of the Republika Srpska. During the Defence case, the Defence will present ample additional evidence to corroborate this statement. You will hear, furthermore, that in 1994, when he returned to that position, he removed some leading individuals from the police and that he -- that -- and that he tried to establish responsibility for all crimes that had been committed, particularly war crimes, and that he insisted on arresting perpetrators of war crimes. You will hear about his fight against crime in general, which is why he clashed with the political leadership and that's why he was removed from his position for the second time. Most particularly, you will hear the testimony about the moment when this Tribunal's indictment was served on Mico Stanisic in 2005 and his reaction and attitude towards the indictment. During the Defence case, you will hear additional evidence about Mico Stanisic's work and efforts invested by himself and his closest associates to introduce the rule of law in the territory of the Republika Srpska. His positions, actions and conduct are typical of a man who does not wish to inflict harm upon anybody, or embarrassment. On the contrary, they show him as a serious and responsible civil servant and state official who did everything in his power, at the expense of his own personal safety and the safety of his associates, to protect public order and security and offer protection to all citizens of the Republika Srpska irrespective of their ethnic affiliation, which was his duty under the law. During its case, the Defence intends to demonstrate that there is no evidence to corroborate the Prosecution allegations from the indictment or a shred of evidence for any of the crimes the Prosecution charges the accused, Mico Stanisic, with. When I say that, I mean Counts 4 through 11, and 17 through 23 of the indictment. We intend to show that there is no evidence in this case that Stanisic is individually criminally responsible, under Article 7(1) of the ICTY Statute, for the crimes under Articles 3 and 5 of the Statute with which he is charged in this indictment, and which he allegedly committed not directly but as a co-perpetrator, and which he aided and abetted and assisted in their planning, preparation or commission. Let me be quite open, Your Honours. It is Mr. Stanisic's position that there was no joint criminal enterprise as described in the indictment or in any other way which he would have been a member of or whose common purpose he would have shared. It is his position that the evidence adduced to date and that which is yet to be presented during the Defence case demonstrate that Mico Stanisic was not involved in any criminal activity, individually or in concert with others, or any sort of conspiracy or criminal enterprise. He fulfilled his obligations under the laws in force at the time responsibly and as far as it was possible for him to do so. Furthermore, as minister of the interior, he did not do anything impermissible or criminal, either through action or inaction. Quite the contrary, in fact. The joint criminal enterprise, as pleaded in the indictment, which ties it in with the 24th of October, 1991, as the date when the Assembly of the Serbian People in the -- in Bosnia-Herzegovina was established, did not exist. Or if such a joint criminal enterprise or something similar did exist, Mico Stanisic was most certainly not a member of that joint criminal enterprise. Furthermore, in our submission, Mico Stanisic did not use physical perpetrators for the commission of any crimes. We will particularly and specifically demonstrate that there is no evidence to support the OTP contentions that, in the municipalities listed in the indictment, and through his action, and inaction, Mico Stanisic did as follows. Under A, participating in the formation of the Bosnian Serb bodies and forces that implemented the forcible takeovers of the municipalities and participated in the crimes listed in this indictment. Under B, participating in the development of Bosnian Serb policy at the leadership level in order to secure the takeovers of the municipalities in the targeted territory and the forcible removal of the non-Serb population. Under C, communicating and coordinating with Bosnian Serb political figures at the republican level, particularly Karadzic and Krajisnik, as well as political, military, and police figures at the regional and municipal levels, in order to facilitate the implementation of the objective of the joint criminal enterprise. Under D, commanding over members and agents of the RS MUP in implementing the objective of the joint criminal enterprise. Under E, assisting in the co-ordination of joint operations of the Army of Republika Srpska and the MUP of Republika Srpska in support of the implementation of the objective of the joint criminal enterprise. Under F, facilitating the establishment and operation of camps and detention facilities in which Serb forces beat, killed and sexually assaulted non-Serb detainees. Under G, failing, while under a duty under the laws and regulations applicable to the Ministry of Interior, to protect the entire civilian population within the areas under the control of Bosnian Serb authorities, to take adequate steps to ensure that MUP -- that the RS MUP forces would act to protect the Bosnian Muslim, Bosnian Croat, and other non-Serb populations residing in those areas. Under H, encouraging and facilitating the commission of crimes by Serb forces against Bosnian Croats, Bosnian Muslims, and other non-Serbs by not taking adequate steps to investigate, arrest, and/or punish the perpetrators of such crimes and thereby contributing to the maintenance of a culture of impunity in respect of such crimes, including by participating in sham inquiries concerning these crimes. Therefore we contest all these allegations from the indictment as indicated above. Furthermore, we intend to demonstrate the following: That did he not have the intent for the commission of any of the crimes listed in the indictment, nor could he have considered them as foreseeable consequences, that he did not have the criminal intent for any of the crimes charged against him. You will hear that, contrary to Prosecution allegations, a certain number of victims listed in the indictment were members of armed forces and not civilians. And, of course, we also contest Mr. Stanisic's responsibility under Article 7(3) of the ICTY Statute. In our submission, the allegations in the indictment are unfounded and incorrect, and the Defence will contest them during its presentation of evidence, just as it did during the Prosecution case. After all, it was for this reason that our client pleaded not guilty, and our pre-trial brief details the underlying reasons. During its case the Defence intends to demonstrate that the Prosecution's allegations and the opinions provided by their experts, Prosecution experts, are erroneous and based on a lack of knowledge of the legal system in force in the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Republika Srpska, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and on a complete and utter misinterpretation of relevant legal provisions. We intend to demonstrate that such allegations are not based on knowledge of relevant issues but, rather, on a one-sided and therefore biased and erroneous interpretation of specific facts which were, for the most part, construed out of the relevant context and legal regulations. We intend to show that there is a significant difference between having knowledge and expertise of a certain field and being merely informed of it through quotations and analyses of selected documents. To give you an illustration of it, let me quote what my learned friend Mr. O'Sullivan had to say about it at some point during this trial: "If I went and designed a bridge after reading all the available material about how to build bridges and without having the requisite knowledge about bridge construction, I would not recommend that you cross that bridge." Your Honours, looking back, I'm sure that, generally speaking, the Trial Chamber has a very clear impression and knowledge of the Defence's position in this case, given that our position has been very transparent and, most importantly, consistent from the start of trial. What we have been maintaining from day one is what we will continue to maintain throughout the Defence case. As I said, the Defence position has not and will not change. In our submission, Mico Stanisic did, indeed, do everything within his powers, obligations, and duties as minister of the interior to combat every type of crime. You have ample evidence to that effect in the record and more will follow. But that is not all. The Defence submits that not only did Mico Stanisic do what was required and necessary, but he did even more than that when the situation was such that it does not bear describing. You have seen and will see that, from day one, not only did he insist in his dispatches on the strict application of the laws and regulations and professional conduct of MUP members, but that he kept repeating it throughout his time as minister and took measures to have his orders and dispatches implemented. We will demonstrate specifically that did not amount to mere correspondence, but that the MUP inspectors present in the headquarters risked their lives at times to oversee the implementation of instructions on the order of the minister and his assistants by going out into the field and touring the same CSBs or SJBs, not once, but several times, to make sure that they were implemented. You will see that all his efforts and persistence resulted in the situation taking a significant turn for the better in the second half of 1992, and that these efforts taken by the entire Ministry of Interior headed by him can by no means be connected in the slightest with any alleged joint criminal enterprise or the commission of any crime from this indictment. Quite the contrary. In this case, through a twist of circumstances, not only do we have testimonies of witnesses from the Prosecution case and more to come in the Defence case, but we also have a large amount of contemporaneous documents, even originals, from the ministry of Republika Srpska, as well as copies of the same documents forwarded by CSBs to the territorial public security stations and follow-up letters checking if the instructions were being complied with. We submit that in such a situation nobody could have done more than had been done. Your Honours, the crimes are many. The victims are many. And all of us, including my client, feel it keenly. However, on the other hand, never lose sight of the fact that the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992 was everything but regular in every sense of the word. There was chaos and whirlpool of civil war, where former neighbours, friends and kin killed each other in cold blood, unfortunately. Not even the best qualified and best organised police forces in the world would be able to handle such situations in the circumstances that are incomparably less extreme despite having fully functional states that keep situations under control. I will not be citing examples here because you know them full well. The important thing here is to understand that at that point in time, in 1992, a functional state simply did not exist. The state was only in the making, as was the state administration, including the Ministry of Interior. As one of the Prosecution witnesses graphically put it, the RS MUP had to be established and I quote, "by starting from the green grass." Meaning from scratch. You will recall that on the issue of communications, the Prosecution put in everything they had to prove that there was normal communication with occasional interruptions until one of their witnesses explained the relations quite plastically in terms of figures. Specifically, that in normal times, the entire MUP traffic of dispatches in Bosnia-Herzegovina amounted to over 300.000 dispatches a year, and that in 1992, the RS MUP, at a time when armed clashes raged, had only 8.570 of them all together. The fact of the matter is that three CSBs of the RS MUP did not even exist before April 1992, that they were yet to be established and to be made to work at a basic level, that -- I -- I will remind you that active policemen were by far a minority compared to reservists, who were picked out and placed on the police reserve force by Crisis Staffs or other organs wholly unrelated to the MUP. In our submission, when all these issues are taken into account, one can hardly point a finger and say that this ministry, or this minister, did not do this and that in 1992 and had the ability to do so. Surely the Trial Chamber will recall that on several occasions during the Prosecution case, I underscored the fact that, from the very start, the Defence left no room for doubt as to which witnesses would be called during the Defence case, and that, aside from Defence experts, most of them would be witnesses whom the Prosecution had placed on their 65 ter lists but did not call to testify. I use lists in plural here because these lists were amended on several occasions at trial, as we all know, with new witnesses being added, others dropped, only to subsequently reappear. And the Prosecution did not call these witnesses to testify. Hence, the case will proceed just as I announced it. During the Defence case, the Chamber will hear two experts, that is, an expert on police matters who is a professor at a police academy. Therefore, a fully competent witness who will provide detailed explanations and clarifications of the legal provisions governing internal affairs in the relevant period, specifically the establishment of the MUP of Republika Srpska in Bosnia-Herzegovina; the way the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina worked in 1990 to 1992; the duties, rights and obligations of MUP members and the ministry as a whole; the system of management within the RS MUP; the duties, rights and obligations of the minister and other senior officials under the law in force; the disciplinary and criminal responsibility of MUP members as provided for in the regulations in force at the time, in terms of powers to request, initiate, conduct, render decisions, and the appeals procedure. I mean the appeal in the disciplinary proceedings. In particular, the expert sets out in his report a comparison between the de jure and de facto situations in respect of all the specific issues I mentioned above and addresses some of the conclusions drawn by Prosecution experts. In the supplement to his report, the expert addresses the only two topics that are, in our view, material and relevant for this case and which have to do with the report of the Prosecution's military expert. The second expert of the Defence is also a university professor, a demographer whose main area of study is precisely demography in theoretical terms and, more specifically, the demography of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Thus, a fully competent witness too. What I mean to say is that the expert addresses in his report the history, mechanisms, reasons, and courses of migrations in Bosnia-Herzegovina over time and specifically during the period relevant to the indictment. Crucially, the expert gives a comprehensive view of the issue and provides explanations from the perspective of the entire population of Bosnia-Herzegovina and not just individual groups, because, as we noted previously, and repeatedly, we believe that the type of report which relates to individual groups, which is the sort of report presented by the Prosecution, inevitably implies bias and means that the subject of study is examined out of context. Consequently, such a report runs contrary to the basic principles of scientific methodology. The Defence intends to call fact witnesses relevant to this indictment. They may roughly be divided into three groups, depending on the issues they will testify to. Two witnesses will testify about the situation in the security services centres. One of the witnesses was a CSB chief and the other a chief of the CSB crime service. In selecting witnesses, the Defence has primarily focussed on members of the crime prevention administration and specifically the crime service, because it is precisely this administration that is believed to be in the best position to provide relevant information about the crimes listed in the indictment. The Trial Chamber will surely recall that under the Law on Internal Affairs of Republika Srpska, the MUP of Republika Srpska of Bosnia-Herzegovina was organised into five Security Services Centres; namely, Trebinje, Sarajevo, Bijeljina, Banja Luka, and Doboj. You will also recall that, previously, the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina had had nine Security Services Centres. In other words, of the CSBs that had existed before the conflicts in April and May of 1992, only the CSBs in Banja Luka and Doboj remained in the territory of Republika Srpska. Given that in terms of hierarchy the CSBs come directly under the MUP headquarters, the Defence intends to have the most competent witness possible, a CSB chief, present to the Chamber the way the centre worked before and after the split in the MUP and before and after the armed clashes in the territory of that centre. Since our choice was significantly reduced due to the fact that, as I said, of the five CSBs in the Republika Srpska, only two had existed before the split in the MUP, and in view of the fact that Mr. Zupljanin is a co-accused in this case, we were left only with the chief of CSB Doboj, who meets both these criteria. Therefore, our first witness will Mr. Andrija Bjelosevic, chief of the state security centre during the time relevant to this case. The area covered by CSB Doboj includes, among others, three municipalities from the indictment; namely, Doboj, Teslic, and Bosanski Samac. Through his testimony and the documents we will present during his evidence, the witness will explain in detail the situation in the CSB area before the split in the MUP, the failure to operate as well as the unlawful activity of the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He will also explain the processes unfolding at the time and state his reasons for attending the meeting in Banja Luka on the 11th of February, 1992. He will give first-hand testimony of the relations between the Crisis Staffs and CSB chiefs. He will testify about the actual state of affairs in CSB Doboj and his engagement in the army under the command of Colonel Lisica, as well as about the relations or the attitude of the army toward the civilian authorities. The witness will also discuss the problems he confronted in his work during the armed clashes in 1992 and CSB's lack of control over the territory in the first several months. He will testify about his presence at the first RS MUP collegium meeting in Belgrade on the 11th of July and about all the other collegium meeting he attended during the period relevant to the indictment, including the issues and problems discussed at these meetings. Furthermore, the witness will testify about the measures he took to functionally unify CSB Doboj, about when the centre started to operate properly, when it created a network with local SJBs on the ground along the various lines of work, and about the measures of control and supervisory inspection that were implemented in these SJBs. He will also discuss the resistance he met from local authorities on the issue of appointments and removals of individuals in leadership positions in the territory. The witness will also testify about the supervisory inspection and tours of CSBs by inspectors from the MUP headquarters on several occasions in the autumn of 1992. Finally, the witness will speak about the measures taken by the CSB to file criminal reports for crimes committed against non-Serbs, to impose disciplinary measures against certain members of the centre, and reasons why such measures were not taken against other members of CSB and the subordinated SJBs. This witness was interviewed by the Prosecution on more than one occasion. Witness Simo Tusevljak is also a professional policeman. He had been working in the crime service of the city of Sarajevo SUP since the 1st of September, 1990. During that time, he was coordinator for general crime for the town of Sarajevo. The witness will testify how, during this period, there was, at the same time, an upward trend in the number of crimes and a decline in the number of uncovered cases of crime and will give the reasons behind this state of matters.
