He will further testify about the makeup of the police personnel who were employed during this period, and I mean with the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You will also hear detailed information about illegal arming and arms trafficking in the town of Sarajevo, and about the deliberate coverup of these crimes by some of the MUP members. He will give evidence about the existence of a separate parallel system of communications that the Muslim members of the MUP had together with the paramilitary organisation the Green Berets, and about the situation in Sarajevo on the 1st of March, 1992. He will also testify about the events in Sarajevo in early April 1992. He will testify about his knowledge of the split in the MUP and what sort of instructions existed in that regard. From June 1992 onwards, the witness was chief of the crime service of the CSB Sarajevo of MUP of Republika Srpska, Bosnia-Herzegovina. He will further testify about the situation in the field, the number of employees and stations, police participation in combat operations, and measures taken to set up a crime service. The witness will give evidence about the situation in the field and whether the CSB was able to control the stations in the field and, in particular, about the meetings with SJB chiefs and instructions given on these occasions. In particular, the witness will speak about the situation in the stations across CSB territory and about the problems they confronted in their work. The witness will give evidence about the work of the judiciary at this time and in that territory, and about the relations with the army. The witness will particularly speak about the criminal reports filed against perpetrators of crimes, reports against MUP members, and about the way in which KU registers were kept. The next group of witnesses that the Defence will call are from the MUP headquarters and they include the chief of the crime prevention administration, Mr. Goran Macar who took up the position following the month of July 1992, after Prosecution Witness ST-220 was removed. As an experienced policeman, the witness will give evidence about his work in the MUP of Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as of 1977, about his acquaintance with Mico Stanisic, and about what his opinion was of Mico Stanisic back then. He will further testify about his work in Sarajevo as chief for general crime as of 1990, that being the position he held at the time of the events in early April 1992, and about the way the Serbian Democratic Party treated him. The witness will give evidence about his joining the RS MUP and the positions he held. In particular, the witness will testify about the first review of the RS MUP personnel in Sokolac on the 30th of March, 1992, a glimpse of which you saw in the video footage which he attended. He will also speak about the early days of the crime sector administration and the number of inspectors he used to have in the administration back at the HQ. The witness will give evidence about the establishment of this administration in Bijeljina and its initial relatively normal work in the autumn of 1992, when inspectors were being dispatched into the field for supervisory inspection and in order to learn about the situation on the ground. The witness will speak, in particular, about the tour of CSB Banja Luka in mid-November 1992 and about the visit of a group of inspectors to SJB Prijedor which he headed, and I mean he headed the group of inspectors. The witness will further testify about the objective problems MUP was confronted with due to the absence of records of MUP members, the migration of the population in 1992, and the background to several orders issued by the minister to remove those MUP members who did not deserve to be on the MUP force, to downsize the reserve force and to place these MUP members at the disposal of the VRS. The witness will also give evidence about the first time that the MUP HQ toured the CSB in Banja Luka in March 1993, and his conclusion about the state of crime in that CSB at the time with reference to the crime at Koricanske Stijene. The witness will testify about the initiative taken by the MUP to prosecute war crimes at a time when Mico Stanisic was minister for the second time around. The witness was interviewed by the Prosecution and was on the Prosecution 65 ter witness list as ST-118. Witness Dragan Andan was a police inspector of the RS MUP. Before the outbreak of armed clashes, he occupied a very senior position in the BH MUP as a senior inspector first-class of the police administration charged with public law and order. His line of duty was to control the work of SJBs in East Herzegovina. The witness will give evidence about the situation in the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the ministry's collapse after the multi-party elections. He will describe the examples of a number of SJBs across the territory of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He will testify how Muslim leaders of the MUP, Avdo Hebib above all, placed ethnicity before profession, and how the split along the ethnic lines within the BH MUP began as early as during the time of Minister Muhamed Besic, who held this position before Alija Delimustafic. He will testify about the barricades in Sarajevo on 1st of March, 1992, and the information available to the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time about the organisers of barracks. He will give evidence about his knowledge of Mico Stanisic in relation to this event, and what sort of man Mico Stanisic was reputed to be, as well as about the reasons for Mico Stanisic's removal from the position of the chief of the city of Sarajevo SUP. The witness was in favour of keeping a united MUP and opposed the split. He will also testify about the dilemmas he faced in that regard. How his dilemmas were dispelled and why he decided to flee Sarajevo and when. When he crossed over to the MUP of Republika Srpska of Bosnia-Herzegovina, he was posted to Bijeljina as an inspector. He was dispatched from Bijeljina to try to sort the situation out in the SJB Brcko. He will testify about the situation he found there and measures he took, as well as about conflicts with certain groups in Brcko. He will also speak about his knowledge of the Luka prison and under whose authority it was. Following his time in Brcko, he was sent back to Bijeljina to sort the matters there, together with a team of the federal SUP led by Mico Davidovic, Prosecution Witness ST-142. He will testify about the situation in Bijeljina and the role played by Dusko Malovic's group. He spent sometime there as acting chief of the public security station, or of the CSB, and has knowledge about the powers over the Batkovici camp near Bijeljina; it's a military camp. He will give evidence about the original way in which he set about implementing the minister's order to downsize the police reserve force. He will further testify about how he prepared, organised and reconnoitred the Zvornik area for the operation against the Yellow Wasps, which was a success. He personally arrested Zuco. He will testify about the praise he received from the minister for that and for preparing a similar operation in Foca. He will also testify about the reasons about why it was aborted. He will testify about the encounter with ST-171 and the subject of discussions at the time in 1992. He will testify about how a disciplinary procedure was initiated against him and how he stopped working in the MUP of Republika Srpska. The witness will also give evidence about Mico Stanisic calling him in 1994 and asking that he rejoin the MUP to lead a team for combatting all manner of crime, including war crimes and arresting perpetrators of war crimes. The witness will testify that he was appointed police director of Republika Srpska in 2004, and that during the two years he performed this duty, 11 individuals were brought before this Tribunal, including Mico Stanisic. The witness himself served Mico Stanisic with the indictment and he will testify to this event. He was interviewed by the Prosecution and IPTF on several occasions. He was proposed as Witness ST-122. Witness Milomir Orasanin is a 92 ter witness. He is a professional policeman. He was an inspector in the MUP of RS of UZSK, which is the administration for crime prevention. He was one of the inspectors from the administration headed by Goran Macar until November 1992, when he transferred to the border police administration. He will testify about knowing Mico Stanisic from the school days. He will testify about the sidelining of Serbian members of the MUP and arming of the Green Berets in Novo Sarajevo, where he was chief of the crime prevention department. The arming escalated with the attack by the Green Berets on SJB on the 4th of April, 1992. He will give evidence about the situation in the RS MUP as he found it in May 1992, when he joined the RS MUP, and about the problems they faced. The witness was present at a meeting in mid-1992 between Mico Stanisic and some members of the crime prevention administration and will testify about what was discussed at the time and what it was that Minister Stanisic insisted on. He participated in drafting the instructions on the deposit and war crimes. He will give evidence about his visit for supervisory inspection to Ilijas and Vogosca in May and about the situation he found there. In June he went on a supervisory inspection visit to Skelani, Zvornik and Brcko. He will testify about the situation he found there and about the supervisory inspection in the area of CSB Doboj in August. He will also speak about the visits to SJBs in Foca, Rudo and Visegrad. The witness was interviewed by the Prosecution. Nikola Milanovic is a 92 ter witness as well. He is also one of the crime prevention administration inspectors, Orasanin's colleague. He will testify about his acquaintance with Mico Stanisic and about his work together in the SUP Sarajevo for the whole of 15 years. He will testify about Mico Stanisic's attitude toward members of other ethnicities. He will speak about how he was pensioned off for being a Communist and member of the Serbian People on two occasions, in 1991 and 1992, how he complained to the SDS president Karadzic about the treatment he was accorded by the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and what sort of measures Karadzic took in response to that. The witness wrote what was probably the first criminal report by RS MUP, and against a Serb at that, for the crime of murder committed against a Muslim in the Lukavica area. He will testify about supervisory inspection carried out in 1992 and the situation as he found it on the ground. He was interviewed by the Prosecution on several occasions and was on their 65 ter list as ST-120. Because of his impaired health, it was submitted that he should testify via videolink. The third group of witnesses are individuals who can provide information about specific events or issues which came to the fore during the Prosecution case and which remain a matter of contention between the parties. Witness Branko Vlaco retired from the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina back in 1989. He subsequently lived in Vogosca where he kept a catering establishment at the time. As the conflict broke out he was in France on a temporary job, but since his family resided in Vogosca, he returned right away. The witness became a member of the Vogosca Crisis Staff. The Crisis Staff, or more specifically, Zdravko Luketa appointed him warden of the reception centre called Naka's Garage. The reception centre was subsequently moved to the location called Bunker, and to Sonja's cafe, called Kontiki. The witness will say under whose control these reception centres were. After the KPD Butmir department was set up at the location called Planja's house, he was appointed warden of the department in Vogosca by virtue of a decision issued by the Ministry of Justice on the 21st of July, 1992. The witness will testify about how there was another individual with a similar first name and identical last name who was a member of the MUP. The witness will also give evidence about how he joined the RS MUP only on the 1st of October, 1992. The witness does not have a passport and there is a procedure pending against him before the High Court in Belgrade as well as a possible investigation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. For these reasons he cannot appear before the Chamber and it was submitted that he should testify via videolink. The Defence intends to include two 92 quater witnesses, both of whom are from Bosanski Samac. In the relevant period witness Stevan Todorovic was appointed chief of SJB Samac by the Crisis Staff. His testimony was partially admitted during the Prosecution case, and the portion of his testimony that the Defence intends to rely on is tendered under Rule 92 quater. Todorovic's testimony is relevant to the role the Crisis Staff played in his appointment, activity, reporting, and responsibility. The testimony is also relevant to the events alleged in this indictment. Witness Stoko Sekulic, also from Bosanski Samac, was a member of the MUP before the armed clashes in March/April 1992. He testifies about the situation in the SJB after Stevan Todorovic took up his position as the chief and about Stevan Todorovic's conduct during that time. He was appointed to the post of SJB commander in the summer of 1992 under a certain degree of pressure from Todorovic. He introduced a degree of order into the work of the station whose functioning up to that point left much to be desired. The witness gives evidence about supervisory inspection conducted by inspectors from CSB Doboj and the RS MUP. He also testifies about the army arresting Stevan Todorovic in November 1992 and the appointment of a new SJB chief thereafter. Moreover, as you know, the Defence intends to adduce 895 documents from our 65 ter list to corroborate the statements that will be made or have already been made by witnesses or experts. Finally, Your Honours, we submit that Mico Stanisic is not a man who is capable of committing the crimes the Prosecution has charged him with. At no point during his life has he exhibited any manner of intolerance, extremism, hatred, inclination to violence or indeed violence itself. This transpires quite clearly from his conduct during the whole of 56 years of his life, from what he did and how did he it, and from what he said. The facts thereof are either before you already or will be presented during the Defence case. He is a man who has always insisted on the consistent application of law and professionalism. Crime is the last thing Mico Stanisic would justify, regardless of who committed it and what the motives were. As he, himself, has said on several occasions, his conscience is clear. He has been saying from the moment he was indicted that the Prosecution allegations and charges are unfounded. He asserts that these allegations and charges are without foundation and utterly erroneous. Mico Stanisic believes that the evidence that has been adduced so far and that which has yet to be presented to the Chamber will give a clear picture and completely answer all the charges against him, and that at the end of this trial you will acquit him of these charges. Thank you, Your Honours. These were my opening statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Zecevic, for your opening remarks. The Chamber has taken good notice of the evidence that you have accounted for and that will come to us in the next couple of months. There is one matter that I wanted to raise before we hear the Defence witnesses. And as you will recall, it is a matter that we also addressed when the Prosecution was leading its witnesses; namely, the issue of whether the parties would be willing to offer to the Chamber copies of the witness statements to the extent, of course, that such statements exist. You drew our attention to the fact that you will be leading several witnesses who were originally scheduled as Prosecution witnesses, and I suppose that for those witnesses, very likely, statements do exist, taken by the Prosecution originally. And maybe there are, for those and for other witnesses, additional statements that have been taken by you. It is of assistance to the Chamber to see these statements before we hear the witnesses so as to give the Judges a better idea of the testimony that these witnesses will bring. And we ask for this, not to have those pieces exhibited and admitted into evidence, but, rather, as a supplement and as a support to the accounts that you have made in your Rule 65 ter submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the situation is as follows. Concerning two 92 ter witnesses which we proposed, the -- none of them gave a statement. They have their -- their interviews given to the Office of the Prosecutor. We want to rely on that, and we offer that as a part of the package. One of the witnesses gave an additional statement, and it's also a part of the package and it's already disclosed to Your Honours. As all other witnesses, none of them gave any statements, although they were on the -- a majority of them were on the -- on the list of the Office of the Prosecutor, they never gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, and, as far as I can remember, they were offered as viva voce witnesses. However, their interviews given to the Office of the Prosecutor do exist, and we don't see any -- any particular problem in disclosing these -- these interviews given to the Office of the Prosecutor to -- to the Trial Chamber, except if maybe Office of the Prosecutor has something in opposition to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I have a concern and a question, I guess. The interviews that were given to the Prosecution that did not result in any statements being created were generally tape-recorded conversations. And you've seen or heard some of these transcripts of those. I guess I'm wondering out loud is the Defence saying that they took no statements from any of their witnesses? There are no witness statements other than, I think, the one that has been disclosed? If they have investigator notes or tape-recorded interviews of their witnesses and they're willing to disclose those to the Trial Chamber, then that would affect our position as to what we want to do. So no notes ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We don't have any notes, nor recorded interviews. We relied on their interviews given to the Office of the Prosecutor and based on that, we spoke to -- to the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And took no notes or tape-recorded none of those conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, none.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Oh. Your Honour, we're in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So in that case -- thank you very much, Mr. Hannis. In that case, we would be much obliged if the Defence would make these transcripts available to the Judges before the witnesses appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we take the break now and you will be ready with your witness when we resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes, the witness is scheduled to come tomorrow morning at 9.00, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we take the adjournment to 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 12th day of April, 2011, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25
